```{r}
#| label: setup-method

source("R/site.R")
provenance <- stat_table("provenance")
have <- !is.null(NUMBERS)
```

This page describes how `lowpoly-pdf-to-svg` turns a papercraft template into a cut file, and
how a person and the program share the work of getting it right. The program does every step it
can check itself and fixes what it can prove. It asks the person only about what it cannot
decide. Every answer is saved, applied on each later build, and used to train the number reader.
The numbers below come from the Bowser model on the current `main` branch.

The design rests on one observation. A low-poly template carries more than its picture. Every
printed edge number appears exactly twice, once on each of the two edges that are glued
together. The two edges must be the same length, one of them must sit on a glue tab, and the
finished model must fold up and close. These rules let the program check its own trace without
any ground truth. Tracing alone, judged by how close the picture looks, cannot catch these
errors. The [benchmark](benchmark.qmd) shows that visual metrics barely react to them.

## Pipeline

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "One build (`make`). Grey boxes run without a person; the check page is the only step that needs one, and its saved files feed the next build."
flowchart TD
  pdf[PDF template] --> render[1 Render pages]
  render --> detect[2 Detect pieces, cuts, folds, number marks]
  detect --> read[3 Read numbers: Tesseract + digit matcher]
  read --> hand[4 Apply saved hand fixes]
  hand --> joint[5 Joint repair: look-alikes, mirror twins]
  joint --> check[6 Self-checks: pairs, junctions, scale, 3D fold-up]
  check --> out[Inkscape SVG, edge table, status page]
  check --> cards[7 Check page: only what is left in doubt]
  cards -- "corrections, lines, piece fixes" --> hand
  cards -- "corrected digits" --> read
```

### 1 Render

`pdftoppm` renders each page listed in the project YAML at 180 dpi. The YAML assigns each page
to a cardstock colour and names the fold styles the template uses. All later geometry is in
millimetres, using the page's own scale.

### 2 Detect

The template prints three kinds of ink, and `detect.py` separates them:

* **Cut lines** are solid grey strokes that enclose each piece. A piece is the background area
  fully enclosed by cut lines. Its outline is traced and then reduced to corner points joined by
  straight segments, because a low-poly piece has no curves. Each segment is fitted to the
  printed line, and a corner is kept only where the ink turns.
* **Fold lines** are dashed (valley) or dash-dot (mountain) grey strokes. Dashes are thinned to
  centrelines and merged when collinear. Each fold is refitted to its dashes and stretched from
  cut to cut, ending on a corner. Its style is read from the dash pattern under it.
* **Edge numbers** are the darkest ink. Glyphs are grouped into number marks, and each mark is
  attached to the cut edge or tab fold it labels. Ink that belongs to no piece stays on the
  Review layer, so nothing disappears silently.

### 3 Read numbers

Every number mark goes to two readers. Tesseract reads it in both orientations. A small digit
matcher is trained on the page itself, using digits from reads Tesseract is sure of plus every
digit a person has corrected. A reading is accepted when both readers agree, or when Tesseract
alone is very sure (confidence 93 or higher).

The remaining marks are settled together, not one at a time. Since every number is printed
twice, an uncertain mark prefers a close candidate reading that completes a pair. Any number
not printed exactly twice is flagged.

### 4 Apply saved fixes

Three files in the model folder hold what a person has decided. Each build applies them after
reading, so nothing has to be corrected twice.

| file | holds | matched by |
|---|---|---|
| `bowser-corrections.csv` | what a number should say (or that it is not a number) | the nearest mark on that piece, within 2 mm |
| `bowser-pieces.csv` | folds added or dropped, corners moved | the nearest fold or corner |
| `bowser-lines.csv` | the line a number marks, drawn by hand | the number's mark |

After a piece changes, its numbers look for their lines again.

### 5 Joint repair

Each edge number is now checked against its partner. The edge table (`bowser-edges.csv`)
gives every number one status: *ok* (one plain edge and one tab, lengths within 1 mm),
*unpaired*, *length mismatch*, *no tab*, *both tabs* or *extra copy*. Two kinds of evidence then
fix numbers without asking.

**Look-alike misreads.** Take a number that did not pair up. If an unpaired line of the same
length on the other side (edge against tab) carries a number that looks like a misreading of it,
the two are matched. The evidence is OCR's own second choice, or a single differing digit. A
match is applied only when it is clear-cut: OCR offered the suggested number, the lines agree
within 0.3 mm, neither copy has another candidate, and the suggested number has no clean pair
yet. In addition, either the read number already pairs elsewhere, or the copy being fixed was a
shaky read (confidence below 80) while its partner was not. Any other match becomes a suggestion
for the person.

**Mirror twins.** Most pieces have a mirror twin cut from the same cardstock. Twins are found
by walking round each piece and comparing the lengths of its numbered lines with another
piece's lengths walked the other way. An *exact* mirror also matches tab for tab; a *variation*
has its tabs on other edges. Pairing every numbered line with its mirror line gives three
checks:

* A line and its mirror should be the same length; if not, one was traced wrongly.
* A fold on one twin with nothing at the mirror place on the other is probably a missed fold.
* Glue pairs mirror too, so a clean pair on one side predicts the number on the other side.

### 6 Self-checks

`checks.py` looks for faults that need no ground truth:

* a fold that meets the cut between two corners (a corner was missed);
* a cut line that runs on past a traced corner (the corner was clipped);
* a piece traced twice, or a tiny outline with no folds or numbers;
* a page whose glued pairs are all slightly longer or shorter than their partners (a scale error).

Each fault is written to the edge table at the numbers it touches.

The 3D fold-up (`make -f fold3d.mk`, [3D fold-up](fold3d.qmd)) is the strongest check. It
folds every piece along its scores, glues each numbered pair and measures the gap left. A
misread number or a mis-traced line usually shows up as a glue that will not close.

```{r}
#| label: auto-summary
#| output: asis
if (have) {
  cat(sprintf(paste(
    "On Bowser, the program read %d numbers on %d pieces. It was sure of %d without help.",
    "It fixed %d further numbers itself: %d look-alike misreads and %d predicted from mirror twins.",
    "Mirror twins pair up %d numbered lines (%d of them on exact twins); %d differ in length from their mirror line.",
    "The self-checks flag %d trace faults."),
    stat("numbers"), stat("pieces"), stat("ocr_sure"),
    stat("auto_fixed"), stat("auto_lookalike"), stat("auto_mirror"),
    stat("mirror_lines"), stat("mirror_exact"), stat("mirror_differ"), stat("trace_faults")))
  if (!is.na(stat("glue_total"))) cat(sprintf(" In the 3D fold-up, %d of %d glued edges close.",
                                              stat("glue_closes"), stat("glue_total")))
  cat("\n")
}
```

## Human in the loop

The aim is that the person spends time only where the program is unsure, and that each answer
improves later reads as well as fixing this one. The review happens on one local page,
`app/number-check.html`. `make fix` writes its data (`bowser-check.json`, with crops of the scan,
which stays local because the pattern is personal-use only). The page opens the model folder and
saves straight back into it.

### What the person is asked

The program sorts what it found into cards. Each card shows the scan around the number beside
the scan around its partner, with the traced line drawn on both.

| card | when | the person |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed for you | a clear-cut look-alike or mirror fix was applied | can glance and override; no answer needed |
| Suggested | a likely misread, not clear-cut enough to apply | confirms the suggestion or types the right number |
| Doubt | a hand correction that still does not pair | rechecks the correction, its partner or the line |
| Open | a number with no explanation | types the number, marks it *not a number*, or draws its line |

A hint on each suggestion says whether the 3D fold-up agrees: the two pieces meet when glued on
that number. By default the page shows only open cards. Fixes the program made itself are
listed under *Fixed for you*.

The **piece review** works the same way for geometry. Twin pieces are shown side by side and
sorted by how much likely needs fixing. That score counts trace faults, untraced line ink inside
the piece, numbers that found no fold, and folds the mirror twin has but this piece lacks.
Missing folds are drawn in orange. The person adds or drops a fold, moves a corner, or marks the
piece OK. The style of an added fold is read from the dashes printed under it.

### What happens to an answer

Saving writes the three fix files from step 4. The next build (`make redo`, which reuses the
saved trace of untouched pages) applies them, reruns joint repair and the self-checks, and
rebuilds the cards. Fixing one number can complete a pair, and that can settle a mirror
prediction or close a glue in 3D. One answer often clears more than one card.

Corrections also feed back into reading. Each corrected number teaches the digit matcher its
digits, upright as Tesseract turned them. Freshly traced pages therefore read better than the
first pages did.

```{r}
#| label: fig-provenance
#| fig-cap: "Where each edge number's final reading comes from. *Confirmed* means a person checked the number and kept the reading; *changed* means they typed another one."
#| fig-height: 2.6
if (!is.null(provenance)) {
  provenance |>
    mutate(source = factor(source, c("readers sure", "fixed by the program", "person confirmed",
                                     "person changed", "readers unsure"))) |>
    ggplot(aes(n, fct_rev(source), fill = outcome)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("pairs (ok)" = "#2f6db5", "still open" = "#e8903a")) +
    labs(x = "edge numbers", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: effort-summary
#| output: asis
if (have) {
  cat(sprintf(paste(
    "So far the person has answered %d number cards: %d confirmed the reading and %d changed it.",
    "The piece review holds %d piece edits (%s), and %d lines were drawn by hand (%s).",
    "%d of %d numbers pair cleanly; the rest are still open.\n"),
    stat("cards_answered"), stat("cards_answered") - stat("cards_changed"), stat("cards_changed"),
    stat("piece_edits"), stat("piece_edits_by_action"), stat("lines_drawn"), stat("lines_by_kind"),
    stat("matching"), stat("numbers")))
}
```

### Why the review is split this way

Three rules shape it.

1. **Act only on proof.** A fix is applied without asking only when several independent
   checks agree: the reader's own alternative, matching lengths, a single candidate, and no clash
   with an existing pair. A wrong automatic fix costs more than a question, because a person
   would have to find it first. Every automatic fix stays visible and can be overridden.
2. **Ask with the evidence on screen.** A card shows both copies of the number and the line
   each one marks. The person judges a pair, not an isolated digit.
3. **Keep every answer as data.** Corrections are plain CSV files kept in git. They make builds
   reproducible, they train the reader, and they form the record of human effort that research
   question 3 needs ([#9](https://github.com/tungufoss/lowpoly-pdf-to-svg/issues/9)).

## Research use

The pipeline is the system evaluated in papers 2 and 3. Paper 1 benchmarks existing methods
only.

* **Joint reasoning** ([#8](https://github.com/tungufoss/lowpoly-pdf-to-svg/issues/8)). Each
  repair source can be switched off: pair-up during reading, look-alike fixes, mirror twins,
  self-checks and the 3D hint. Rerunning without one measures what it adds. The ablation runs
  have not been done yet.
* **Correction effort** ([#9](https://github.com/tungufoss/lowpoly-pdf-to-svg/issues/9)). The
  corrections file records what was decided but not how long it took, and not what a
  person would have had to look at without triage. Logging time per card, and replaying the
  saved corrections on an exhaustive review order, is the next step.
